questions.question: What do you like most about your hometown?
questions.sampleAnswer: What I like most is how easy it is to get to know people. I've lived in the same neighbourhood for years, so I usually bump into someone I know when I go out. That gives the place a real sense of community.
vocabulary: neighbourhood — a local area within a town or city
bump into someone — meet someone unexpectedly
sense of community — a feeling of belonging to a local group
structure: Name one thing you genuinely value.
Explain how it makes you feel.

questions.question: Has your hometown changed much in recent years?
questions.sampleAnswer: Yes, quite a bit. There are more apartment buildings now, and a few roads have become much busier. On the positive side, we have a larger public library, which I use fairly often.
vocabulary: quite a bit — considerably
apartment building — a building containing separate homes
on the positive side — introducing an advantage
structure: Describe one or two concrete changes.
Add your reaction to a change.

questions.question: Describe a place in your hometown where you enjoy spending time.
cuePoints: and explain why you enjoy spending time there
questions.sampleAnswer:
I'd like to talk about a small park near the river in my hometown. It's about fifteen minutes from my home on foot, so I can get there without planning a whole outing.

It isn't particularly famous, and there aren't many facilities, but it has a walking path and some old trees that provide plenty of shade. There's also a row of benches facing the water. My favourite one is a little away from the main entrance, where it tends to be quieter.

I usually go there in the late afternoon, especially after a long day of studying. Sometimes I walk around the park with a friend and we catch up on what's been happening. If I go on my own, I might listen to a podcast for a while, although I often end up just watching people and enjoying the view.

What I appreciate most is the change of pace. At home, it's easy to keep checking my phone or thinking about the next task. In the park, I feel less pressure to do something productive every minute. I remember going there before an important exam when I was feeling rather overwhelmed. After a short walk, the problems I'd been worrying about seemed much more manageable.

So, although it's a very ordinary place, it has become part of my routine. I'd certainly miss it if I moved away.
vocabulary: on foot — by walking
catch up — share recent news
a change of pace — a break from your normal routine
overwhelmed — feeling unable to manage everything
structure: Identify the place and how you reach it.
Tell a short personal story and explain its significance.

questions.question: Why are public spaces important in cities?
questions.sampleAnswer: I think they give people somewhere to spend time without having to buy anything. That's particularly valuable in crowded cities, where many residents live in small flats. A park or public square also makes casual social contact possible: people might meet neighbours or take part in a local event. Of course, the space needs to feel safe and be maintained properly if people are going to use it regularly.
vocabulary: casual social contact — informal interaction with other people
maintain — keep something in good condition
residents — people who live in an area

questions.question: Do you prefer studying alone or with other people?
questions.sampleAnswer: I usually prefer studying alone when I need to concentrate, especially if I'm reading something difficult. But I like working with a friend afterwards so we can compare ideas. Explaining something out loud often helps me notice what I haven't understood.
vocabulary: concentrate — give something your full attention
compare ideas — discuss similarities and differences in your views
out loud — so that other people can hear
structure: Mention a situation where the alternative helps.

questions.question: What skill would you like to learn in the future?
questions.sampleAnswer: I'd like to become better at cooking. I can make a few simple meals, but I tend to repeat the same things. It would be nice to try different recipes and feel confident cooking for friends.
vocabulary: tend to — usually do something
recipe — instructions for preparing a dish
feel confident — trust your ability to do something
phrases: I'd like to become better at…
structure: Explain what you would enjoy doing with it.

questions.question: Describe a useful skill you learned from another person.
cuePoints: and explain why it has been useful
questions.sampleAnswer:
A useful skill I learned from someone else was how to organise a household budget. My older cousin taught me shortly before I moved away from home for a course. Until then, I had a fairly vague idea of where my money went.

We sat down with a notebook and listed the costs I could predict, such as rent and transport. Then she helped me estimate what I might spend on food and set aside a small amount for unexpected expenses. What made her explanation helpful was that she used realistic examples rather than telling me simply to spend less.

For the first month, I wrote down everything I bought. That was a bit tedious, but it showed me that small purchases added up much faster than I expected. My cousin checked the figures with me at the end of the month, and we adjusted the plan. I also learned that a budget has to allow some flexibility; otherwise, it's difficult to keep using it.

Since then, I've used a simple spreadsheet instead of the notebook. I don't record every detail quite so carefully now, but I still check my spending once a week. It's useful because I can decide whether I can afford something before I buy it, instead of worrying afterwards.

I wouldn't say I'm an expert with money, but I feel much more in control. It was a very practical lesson, and I'm grateful that she took the time to help me.
vocabulary: set aside — keep something for a particular purpose
unexpected expenses — costs you did not plan for
add up — combine to make a larger total
in control — able to manage a situation
phrases: What made the explanation helpful was…
I wouldn't say I'm an expert, but…
structure: Explain why you needed to learn it.
Describe the learning process with a specific detail.
Explain how you use the skill now.

questions.question: Should adults continue learning after they finish formal education?
questions.sampleAnswer: Yes, because the knowledge we need doesn't stay the same throughout our lives. At work, for example, people may need to learn a new system or take on a different responsibility. Learning can also be enjoyable in its own right, whether that's taking up photography or understanding more about local history. I don't think it always has to mean returning to a classroom; informal practice and guidance from other people can be just as valuable for some skills.
vocabulary: formal education — organised study in schools or colleges
in its own right — valuable by itself
take up — start a new activity
phrases: I don't think it always has to mean…
structure: Give your view and main reason.

questions.question: Is there an app you use every day?
questions.sampleAnswer: Yes, I use a notes app almost every day. I put my shopping lists and study reminders in it, so I don't have to keep everything in my head. It's quite basic, but that's probably why I find it useful.
vocabulary: reminder — something that helps you remember a task
keep something in your head — remember it without writing it down
basic — simple, with essential features
structure: Say what you use it for.

questions.question: Do you ever take a break from your phone?
questions.sampleAnswer: I try to leave it in another room when I'm studying. Otherwise, I tend to check it whenever a task gets difficult. I don't always manage it, but even half an hour without notifications helps me focus.
vocabulary: notification — an alert from a device or app
focus — concentrate on something
tend to — be likely to do something
phrases: I don't always manage it, but…

questions.question: How has technology changed the way people maintain friendships?
questions.sampleAnswer: It has made staying in touch much easier, particularly when friends live in different places. A quick message or video call can help people remain involved in each other's lives without arranging a visit. On the other hand, frequent online contact isn't always the same as having a proper conversation. I think technology works best when it supports a friendship rather than becoming the only way people interact.
vocabulary: stay in touch — continue communicating
remain involved — continue to take part or show interest
interact — communicate or do things with others
phrases: I think it works best when…
structure: Explain an advantage with a concrete example.
